gloss_terse: Garden herb or vegetable; cultivated plant used for food, as opposed to wild-growing vegetation.
gloss_readable: Lachanon refers to cultivated garden plants -- herbs and vegetables grown intentionally for food, in contrast to wild plants that sprout on their own. Jesus uses the mustard seed parable (Matt 13:32; Mark 4:32) to illustrate how the kingdom of God starts as the smallest of seeds yet grows into something larger than all the lachana. In Luke 11:42 the Pharisees tithe even their garden herbs, while in Rom 14:2 it describes the diet of those who eat only vegetables. The word carried everyday, humble associations -- the kitchen garden, not the grand harvest.

senses.1: A cultivated garden plant -- herb or vegetable grown for food. In Jesus' mustard-seed parable (Matt 13:32; Mark 4:32) the plant outgrows all the lachana, emphasizing surprising kingdom growth. Luke 11:42 names specific herbs (mint, rue, garden plants) as objects of Pharisaic tithing, while Rom 14:2 contrasts the vegetable-eater with the meat-eater. Multilingual glosses confirm the culinary sense: Spanish 'hortaliza/legumbres,' French 'légume,' German 'Gemüse' -- all pointing to edible garden produce rather than wild flora.

gloss_terse: Legion; a vast number, originally a Roman military unit of ~5,000 soldiers, used literally and as a name for demonic multitude.
gloss_readable: A Latin loanword that entered Greek through Rome's military presence, legion denotes both a formal Roman army division (roughly 5,000 infantry plus cavalry) and, by extension, an overwhelming multitude. In the Gospels it appears most memorably as the self-identification of a demoniac's possessing spirits: 'My name is Legion, for we are many' (Mark 5:9; Luke 8:30). Jesus also invokes it in Gethsemane, declaring he could summon more than twelve legions of angels (Matt 26:53). The word conveys both organized power and terrifying numerousness.

senses.1: A Roman military unit numbering thousands, used in the NT both literally (of angelic armies, Matt 26:53) and as a proper name for a demonic collective (Mark 5:9, 15; Luke 8:30). The demoniac's self-designation 'Legion' communicates not just plurality but organized, overwhelming force. Spanish 'legión,' French 'Légion,' and German 'Legion' all preserve the Latin military loanword unchanged, reflecting how deeply this Roman institution stamped itself on the Mediterranean world.

gloss_terse: Leprosy; a dreaded skin disease causing scaling and disfigurement, rendering a person ritually unclean under Mosaic law.
gloss_readable: Lepra designates the skin disease that made its sufferers outcasts in ancient Israel -- not necessarily modern Hansen's disease, but a broader category of severe, visible skin afflictions that produced flaking and scaling (the root lepis means 'scale'). Healing a leper was among Jesus' most dramatic signs of messianic authority: he touched the untouchable and pronounced them clean (Matt 8:3; Mark 1:42; Luke 5:12-13). The disease carried enormous social and religious weight, since Levitical law required separation from the community until a priest certified restoration.

senses.1: A severe skin disease characterized by scaling and disfigurement, entailing ritual uncleanness under the Torah. All four NT occurrences appear in healing narratives: Jesus cleanses lepers by touch and command (Matt 8:3; Mark 1:42; Luke 5:12-13), overturning both the physical affliction and its social stigma. French 'lèpre,' Spanish 'lepra,' and German 'Aussatz' (literally 'setting apart') each highlight different facets -- the disease itself or the isolation it imposed.

gloss_terse: Oracle; a divine utterance or saying, especially the collected revelations of God entrusted to Israel.
gloss_readable: Logion (diminutive of logos) denotes a divine saying or oracle -- a word that carries the weight of God's own speech. In the NT it always appears in the plural (logia), referring to the body of God's revelations. Stephen speaks of Moses receiving 'living oracles' at Sinai (Acts 7:38); Paul affirms that the Jews were entrusted with 'the oracles of God' (Rom 3:2). The author of Hebrews chides readers who still need instruction in the basic oracles (Heb 5:12), and Peter urges that anyone who speaks should do so as one delivering God's oracles (1 Pet 4:11).

senses.1: A divine utterance or collected body of God's spoken revelations. In Acts 7:38 Stephen describes Moses receiving 'living oracles' on Sinai -- words pulsing with divine authority. Rom 3:2 names these oracles as Israel's great privilege. Heb 5:12 treats them as foundational teaching, and 1 Pet 4:11 sets them as the standard for Christian speech. French 'oracle' and Spanish 'oráculos' preserve the sacred-pronouncement sense, while German 'Gaben' (gifts) captures the entrusted-treasure dimension.

gloss_terse: To revile, heap verbal abuse on someone; to insult with harsh, contemptuous language.
gloss_readable: Loidoreo describes the act of hurling insults and verbal abuse at someone -- not casual criticism but sharp, contemptuous reviling. In the NT it appears in contexts of unjust hostility: the Pharisees revile the man born blind for following Jesus (John 9:28), Paul is warned against reviling the high priest (Acts 23:4), and both Paul and Christ endure reviling without retaliation (1 Cor 4:12; 1 Pet 2:23). Christ's response to being reviled -- he did not revile in return -- became a paradigm of Christian non-retaliation.

senses.1: To abuse verbally, to heap contemptuous insults on someone. The Pharisees revile the healed blind man as a disciple of Jesus (John 9:28); Paul is rebuked for inadvertently reviling the high priest (Acts 23:4). In 1 Cor 4:12 Paul responds to reviling with blessing, and 1 Pet 2:23 holds up Christ as the model: 'when he was reviled, he did not revile in return.' Spanish 'injuriar/insultar' and French 'injurier/insulter' both capture the wounding, honor-damaging quality of this speech act.

gloss_terse: Lot; Abraham's nephew who settled in Sodom and was rescued before its destruction.
gloss_readable: Lot (Hebrew lot, 'covering' or 'veil') is Abraham's nephew whose story in Genesis serves as a cautionary archetype in the NT. Jesus cites the days of Lot as a parallel to the days of the Son of Man: people were eating, drinking, buying, and selling right up until fire fell from heaven (Luke 17:28-29). The warning 'Remember Lot's wife' (Luke 17:32) became proverbial for the danger of looking back. Peter calls Lot 'righteous' and presents his rescue from Sodom as proof that God knows how to deliver the godly from trial (2 Pet 2:7).

senses.1: The personal name Lot, Abraham's nephew, used in the NT as a typological figure for divine judgment and deliverance. In Luke 17:28-29 Jesus compares the sudden destruction of Sodom in Lot's day to the coming of the Son of Man. Luke 17:32 warns against Lot's wife's backward glance. In 2 Pet 2:7 Lot is called 'righteous,' rescued from the lawless -- a paradigm of God's ability to save the faithful amid catastrophic judgment.

gloss_terse: To make a disciple, train as a follower; to be discipled or instructed in the ways of the kingdom.
gloss_readable: Matheteuo means to make someone a disciple -- to bring them into a relationship of learning and following. Built from mathetes (disciple/learner), this verb carries the full weight of the Great Commission: 'Go and make disciples of all nations' (Matt 28:19). It appears in both active and passive senses: Joseph of Arimathea 'had been discipled' to Jesus (Matt 27:57), a scribe trained for the kingdom draws from treasures old and new (Matt 13:52), and Paul and Barnabas 'made many disciples' in Derbe (Acts 14:21). The verb implies not just initial conversion but ongoing formation.

senses.1: To make someone a disciple or to undergo discipleship training. The Great Commission (Matt 28:19) uses the imperative 'make disciples of all nations,' establishing this as the church's central mission verb. Matt 27:57 describes Joseph of Arimathea as 'having been discipled' to Jesus (passive), while Matt 13:52 pictures a scribe 'discipled for the kingdom.' In Acts 14:21 Paul and Barnabas disciple many in Derbe. Spanish 'hacer discípulos' and French 'devenir disciple' together capture both the active and passive dimensions of the word.

gloss_terse: Soft, fine, delicate; of clothing: luxurious; of persons: effeminate or morally lax.
gloss_readable: Malakos fundamentally means 'soft' -- soft to the touch, fine in texture, delicate in quality. In the Gospels, Jesus contrasts his rough-hewn prophet John the Baptist with those dressed in 'soft garments' (malaka), the kind worn in royal palaces (Matt 11:8; Luke 7:25). The word could also describe moral softness or self-indulgence; in 1 Cor 6:9 Paul uses it in a vice list where it likely denotes those who are morally weak or who yield to sensual excess. The semantic range moves from physical texture to luxury to moral characterization.

senses.1: Soft or fine in texture, and by extension luxurious, effeminate, or morally indulgent. In Matt 11:8 (twice) and Luke 7:25 Jesus asks whether people went to the wilderness to see someone in soft, fine clothing -- the opposite of John's camel-hair garment -- pointing to courtly luxury. In 1 Cor 6:9 the term appears in a vice list with a moral sense: softness as self-indulgent weakness. Spanish 'suaves/afeminados' and French 'mou/délicat' together capture the physical-to-moral spectrum -- from fine fabric to flawed character.

gloss_terse: Mammon; wealth or riches personified, viewed as a rival master to God.
gloss_readable: Mamonas is an Aramaic loanword (mamona, 'wealth' or 'possessions') that Jesus uses to personify riches as a competing lord demanding allegiance. The saying 'You cannot serve God and Mammon' (Matt 6:24; Luke 16:13) frames the choice as absolute -- two masters, two loyalties. In Luke 16:9 Jesus paradoxically urges using 'unrighteous mammon' to make friends for eternity, and in Luke 16:11 faithfulness with mammon becomes a test of fitness for true riches. The word's Aramaic origin gives it an almost demonic resonance in Greek ears.

senses.1: Wealth or material possessions personified as a rival deity or master. Jesus declares that no one can serve both God and Mammon (Matt 6:24; Luke 16:13), framing the pursuit of riches as a form of idolatry. In Luke 16:9, 11 he speaks of 'unrighteous mammon' and 'faithful in mammon,' treating wealth as a proving ground for spiritual trustworthiness. The Aramaic origin is preserved across all translations -- Spanish 'Mamón,' French 'Mammon,' German 'Mammon' -- none domesticate it, preserving its foreignness and its ominous overtone as a power that competes with God.

gloss_terse: Manna; the miraculous bread-like food God provided Israel in the wilderness, later a type of heavenly sustenance.
gloss_readable: Manna -- from the Hebrew man hu ('What is it?') -- is the mysterious food God rained down daily for Israel's forty wilderness years. In the NT it functions typologically: Jesus contrasts the manna the fathers ate and still died with the true bread from heaven that gives eternal life (John 6:31, 49). Hebrews 9:4 recalls the golden jar of manna stored in the ark of the covenant as a memorial of God's provision. In Rev 2:17 the risen Christ promises 'hidden manna' to the faithful overcomer -- a symbol of intimate, eschatological sustenance.

senses.1: The miraculous food God provided daily to Israel in the wilderness, used typologically in the NT for divine and eschatological sustenance. In John 6:31, 49 Jesus contrasts perishable wilderness manna with himself as the living bread from heaven. Heb 9:4 mentions the jar of manna preserved in the ark, a tangible memorial of God's faithfulness. Rev 2:17 promises 'hidden manna' to overcomers -- a rich eschatological image of intimate communion. Spanish 'maná,' French 'manne,' and German 'Manna' all transliterate directly from Hebrew, preserving the original wonder of the question: 'What is it?'
